idiom_name: private constructor + static create()/validateParameters() (Essence collapsed into statics)
implementation_notes: The classic two-class Essence collapses into static members on the CreationTarget itself: a `private` constructor (tsc rejects `new Contract()` outside the class body), plus a `static create()` that validates before instantiating and a `static validateParameters()` for early interactive feedback, with `readonly` fields under `strictPropertyInitialization` guaranteeing compulsory props are assigned exactly once at creation. A type predicate (`p is ContractProps`) certifies the validated property set so `create()` can instantiate without casts, and returning a discriminated union (`Contract | MissingProps`) makes the invalid path a value the caller must handle instead of a constructor exception. Because TypeScript has no friend or package-private, a separate Essence class cannot call the target's private constructor, so the target's own statics take over the Essence role; the classic two-class form is still justified when one validated property set must feed several related CreationTargets or when construction is routed through an injected DDD Factory, which forces a public constructor guarded only at runtime.
pitfalls: `private` constructors and `readonly` fields are compile-time only and erased in emitted JS: plain-JS callers, dynamic imports, or `as unknown as Contract` casts can still bypass the gate - keep a runtime assertion in the constructor as a backstop whenever untrusted code shares the bundle.

TypeScript has no friend/package-private escape, so the literal two-class Essence cannot retrieve values through a private constructor; teams that insist on it must widen the constructor to `public` and thereby delete the entire guarantee - collapse the Essence into static methods instead.

The definite-assignment assertion (`customer!:`) silences strictPropertyInitialization and silently re-opens the partially-initialized hole; TypeScript also does not analyze methods invoked from the constructor, so calling `this.validate()` inside the constructor gives no compile-time certainty of initialized compulsory fields.

Structural typing means an exported `ValidContract` interface is satisfiable by any object literal with the right shape - the guarantee lives only in the non-callable constructor, so never let a validated-typed parameter accept `Partial<Contract>` or leak pre-construction state out of `create()`.

Awaiting validation inside `create()` forces `Promise<Contract>` and re-opens a window where a half-built object exists before validation completes; validate synchronously before any object exists, and reserve async checks for a separate pre-validation step whose result feeds the synchronous gate.
